span.term: Motor-related signals from secondary motor cortex excite PV+ interneurons in auditory cortex, which postsynaptically inhibit excitatory cells and thereby suppress both spontaneous and sound-evoked activity

span.label: distinguishes-from → the disinhibitory account of locomotion-driven gain increases in visual cortex
span.note: differs in: THE AXIS IS THE CIRCUIT MECHANISM, WITH BOTH NAMED. 'THIS MECHANISM CONTRASTS WITH A DISINHIBITORY MECHANISM implicated in locomotion-dependent increases in visual cortical responses, WITH A PARALLEL NEGATIVE RESCALING OF EXCITATORY AND INHIBITORY SYNAPTIC DRIVE that has been advanced to account for STATE-DEPENDENT CHANGES.' Two accounts of behaviour-driven cortical change that predict opposite things about inhibition - so a result reported as `state-dependent modulation` is compatible with either until the inhibitory drive is measured. Q-500.
Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Just before and during locomotion, head movements, grooming and other movements, auditory cortical excitatory neurons showed less variable membrane potentials and a slight depolarization.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: These membrane potential changes began on average more than 200 ms before locomotion started and persisted about as long after it ended.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Because the cortical changes precede movement onset by hundreds of milliseconds, they cannot be caused by sound or other sensory feedback from the movement itself and must instead be motor-related.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Unlike visual cortex, where locomotion boosts responses, tone-evoked synaptic responses of auditory cortical excitatory neurons were significantly reduced during movement.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Roughly 60 percent of the movement-related suppression of tone-evoked responses originates within the auditory cortex itself rather than upstream, since optogenetically evoked thalamocortical responses were suppressed in proportion to tone responses.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The rising slope of thalamocortical EPSPs was unchanged between movement and rest, ruling out presynaptic depression of thalamic terminals as the cause of suppression.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The movement-related membrane potential change reversed near -72 mV, close to the reported chloride equilibrium potential, pointing to a postsynaptic inhibitory (chloride-mediated) current.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Around movement, PV+ and other fast-spiking interneurons in auditory cortex increased their firing while putative excitatory neurons decreased theirs.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The inhibitory neurons' firing rose several hundred milliseconds before movement onset and before excitatory cells dropped below baseline, consistent with inhibition leading the suppression.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Excitatory neurons in secondary motor cortex increased their firing about 870 ms before movement onset, earlier than any of the auditory cortical changes.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Optogenetically activating M2 axon terminals in the auditory cortex of a resting mouse reproduced the movement signature: reduced membrane potential variability, reduced tone-evoked responses and slight depolarization.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The terminal-activation effect was not an indirect antidromic one: it survived pharmacological silencing of M2 cell bodies with TTX.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: The auditory cortical change began within 7 ms of terminal stimulation, faster than the roughly 12 ms antidromic conduction time back to M2, again excluding an indirect route.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Silencing ipsilateral M2 restored rest-like membrane potential dynamics in auditory cortex within about 70 ms of laser onset, before the animal actually stopped moving.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: Silencing ipsilateral M2 while the mouse was still moving recovered about 40 percent of the tone-evoked response, showing M2 activity is necessary for the movement-related gain reduction.
span.note: Quotation withheld because this record is not cleared for redistribution.

span.label: auditory cortical excitatory neurons are suppressed before and during movement, due in part to increased activity of local PV+ interneurons
